title: Mielie Meal Roti
author: Aunty Shantha
desc: Maize meal cooked to a stiff porridge, worked together with cake flour at two parts to one, rolled thin and dry-fried — an Indian bread made from an African grain, and a direct trace of indenture.
longDesc: This is the most quietly remarkable bread in the collection. When rice ran short in the indenture rations, labourers substituted crushed maize — mealie rice — and over generations the substitution worked its way into the bread as well. A roti made of maize meal is not a compromise recipe; it is what happens when a South Asian technique meets a southern African staple and both survive the encounter. The ratio is two cups of maize meal to one of cake flour.
equipment: Mixing bowl, or a food processor with a dough hook
steps: Bring 2 1/2 cups of the water to the boil with the oil and the salt.
Add the maize meal and stir.
Add the remaining water, cover, and cook for 5 minutes.
Reduce the heat and let it steam-cook until stiff.
Tip it into a bowl and add the cake flour.
Work it to a smooth velvety dough — by food processor, dough hook, or by hand, breaking the dough apart and re-gathering it until it comes together.
Roll each out to slightly bigger than a side plate.
Dry-fry over medium heat, turning once, then add butter or ghee after the dry-frying rather than before.
chefTips: Two to one, maize meal to cake flour. Shifting that ratio either way gives you either a bread that cracks or an ordinary roti.
Work the hot porridge properly. The breaking-and-re-gathering is how the flour gets incorporated without lumps, and it takes a few minutes.
Dry-fry first and butter afterwards. Butter in the pan from the start burns before the roti has cooked through.
Roll them thin. A thick mielie meal roti is heavy in a way a wheat one is not.
Work while the dough is still warm. Cold, it crumbles rather than rolls.
commonMistakes: Trying to knead it like a wheat dough, which will not work — maize meal has no gluten to develop.
Letting the dough cool before rolling.
Adding butter to the pan before the roti has set, which burns it.
storage: Wrapped, at room temperature 2 days. They stiffen when cold.
reheating: Warm in a dry pan, briefly on each side.
healthBenefits: Maize meal is naturally gluten-free, though the cake flour here is not.
Lower in fat than a laminated roti, since the butter goes on after cooking.
culturalNote: Mealie rice — crushed dried maize eaten in place of rice — is one of the plainest markers of indenture in the cuisine, and it is worth naming as a poverty adaptation rather than a quirk. That it produced a bread still made by choice, by South African Indian cooks who could buy any flour they like, says something about how completely it was absorbed.
